prose.summary: An account executive owns the number: a patch of accounts or a territory, a quota attached to it, and the decision about which deals get your hours this week. People mix it up with account management, but the split is real: AEs are paid to open and close revenue, account managers are paid to keep it and grow it after the ink dries. Most postings want someone who has already carried a bag for a few years, because the job assumes you know how to run a deal without a script.
prose.day_to_day: The week runs on the pipeline: Monday usually starts with a look at what's committed to close this month and what's slipping, then a run of discovery calls, demos, or renewal check-ins depending on the book you carry. CRM entry (Salesforce for most of these roles) eats more time than anyone admits going in, because a deal that isn't logged doesn't exist to your manager or your forecast. There's a stretch most afternoons for proposal writing or pricing back-and-forth with procurement, and one recurring internal meeting, usually a pipeline review, where you defend your numbers out loud. The part people look forward to is the call where a prospect who's been circling for six weeks finally says yes, or a renewal comes in a size bigger than the last cycle. Roughly half the week is yours alone (research, writing, forecasting); the other half is spent live with buyers or your own team. Fridays tend to be lighter on calls and heavier on cleanup: notes, next steps, updating close dates that everyone knows are optimistic.
prose.work_environment: Close to half of these roles are remote, which fits the actual mechanics of the job: a laptop, a phone line, and a calendar are most of what you need, and buyers are just as willing to take a video call as an in-person one now. The rest split between office-based teams (often because the company wants AEs shoulder to shoulder for coaching and deal strategy) and roles with real travel attached, particularly enterprise accounts where a site visit or an in-person renewal pitch still closes bigger. Hours track the sales calendar more than the clock: quarter-end weeks run long and the last week of the fiscal year can mean nights spent finalizing paperwork before a deal has to land. Outside of that, the schedule is yours to shape as long as the pipeline moves.
prose.getting_in: There's no license here, but there is a soft credential wall: 82% of postings state a degree requirement, though a meaningful share (26%) will waive it for the right track record, and what replaces the degree is usually two or more years of quota-carrying sales experience with numbers to show for it. The median AE has 5 years of experience behind them, and that's the real gate, not the diploma. Most people get there by starting as a sales development rep or sales representative for a year or two, learning to run discovery and handle objections on smaller deals, then moving up to full-cycle ownership of an account list. The stall point is usually right there at that jump: SDRs who can generate meetings but haven't yet closed anything themselves get passed over for AE roles until they can point to a quota they hit. Building a track record at one company and then using it to move to a bigger book elsewhere is the common path, and that jump alone can take a year or more longer than the promotion would have inside the same company.
prose.ladder: The climb is mostly about what you're trusted to carry: first a small book of inbound or SMB accounts, then a defined territory or vertical, then strategic or enterprise accounts where a single deal can be worth what your whole first-year quota was. The first real step up is usually being handed a bigger or more complex territory without needing a manager to co-pilot your calls, which tends to happen once you've hit quota two or three cycles running. From there the ladder forks: some go into sales management, trading their own number for a team's, usually around the 4 to 6 year mark; others stay individual contributors and move into strategic or enterprise AE seats where the pay ceiling can outrun a first-line manager's. Neither fork is a downgrade, it depends on whether you'd rather own other people's pipeline reviews or your own.
prose.suits: People who do well here like the scoreboard: knowing exactly where you stand against a number, every week, and having a bad quarter be recoverable rather than permanent. It suits someone who doesn't need the work to look the same two days running, and who gets something out of the moment a skeptical buyer's questions run out and they start asking about implementation instead of whether they need this at all. It does not suit someone who wants steady, predictable hours or who finds it draining to be told no, repeatedly, by people who never call back. The ones who leave usually wanted the relationship-building parts of the job (the account management, the long-term trust-building) without the quota hanging over it, and they're often much happier moving into customer success once they realize that's what they wanted.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly charm, but the postings lean hard on forecasting, procurement, and negotiation, which is to say the job is arithmetic and paperwork dressed up as relationship-building. Another one: people think AE and account manager are interchangeable titles for the same work, but they sit on opposite ends of the deal, one opens it and one keeps it alive, and companies hire for them separately for a reason.
prose.who_qualifies: Sales representatives are the closest existing role, carrying over the core mechanics of running a deal and living inside a CRM, and the jump from rep to AE is largely about scope: bigger accounts, longer cycles, more of the deal on your own shoulders. Customer success managers also transfer well, since they already know the account, the renewal cycle, and how to defend a number in a business review, though they typically have to build cold outreach and net-new closing muscle they didn't need before. Real estate developers show up as a strong match too, likely because both roles are built around long sales cycles, negotiation, and carrying a deal from first contact to signed contract.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what a specific quota feels like to carry, or whether a territory has been picked over by three AEs before you. It also can't tell you how much of a given comp package is realistic to hit versus a number dangled to get you to sign, which varies wildly by company even when the base and OTE look identical on paper.

steps.do: Land an SDR or junior sales role
steps.how: This is usually the entry point: outbound prospecting, qualifying leads, booking meetings for a closer. Expect 1 to 2 years here before anyone considers you for a full-cycle role, and you're done when you can point to a specific number of meetings booked or pipeline generated.

steps.do: Learn one CRM properly, not casually
steps.how: Salesforce shows up in a quarter of postings and is the default most teams standardize on. Spend real time on pipeline stages, forecasting fields, and reporting, not just data entry, since managers judge your discipline by how clean your CRM hygiene is.

Move into a junior AE or full-cycle sales rep seat where you own a deal from first call to signature. This typically takes another 1 to 2 years and is where you build the track record (quota attainment, deal size, win rate) that gets you taken seriously for a bigger book.

steps.do: Hit and document quota for two cycles
steps.how: Two consecutive quarters or years of hitting or beating your number is the concrete proof point hiring managers ask for. Write down your attainment percentage and average deal size; you'll be asked for both in every interview from here on.

steps.do: Move up to a bigger territory or segment
steps.how: Use your documented quota history to move into mid-market, enterprise, or a named-account territory, either internally or at a new company. This is usually the jump that takes you from the $106k range into six figures higher up the band, and it's done once you're carrying a number nobody had to shrink for you.

prose.tools: Salesforce is the closest thing to a gatekeeper here, showing up in a quarter of postings by name, and not knowing your way around a CRM at all is disqualifying at the interview stage. Beyond that, the job runs on forecasting tools, presentation software for decks and proposals, and whatever procurement or contract system a buyer's company uses on their end, which you learn deal by deal. SaaS-specific sales motion (usage-based pricing, seat expansion, renewal timing) is showing up often enough in postings that it's worth understanding even if your current employer doesn't sell software.

industries.name: SaaS and software
industries.note: Fastest sales cycles, heaviest CRM discipline, and the segment where AE and SDR pipelines are most tightly engineered end to end.

industries.name: Enterprise technology and hardware
industries.note: Longer cycles, bigger deals, more procurement and legal back-and-forth, and travel to the buyer is still common.

industries.name: Financial services and fintech
industries.note: Heavier compliance overhead on every deal and buyers who ask harder questions about security and integration before they'll sign.

industries.name: Real estate and development
industries.note: Deal sizes and negotiation style overlap closely with tech AE work, which is likely why developer and AE roles show up as close matches to each other.

specializations.name: Enterprise / strategic accounts
specializations.why: Deal sizes and comp both scale up sharply here, and companies specifically hire AEs who've proven they can navigate multi-stakeholder procurement rather than promoting internally for every seat.

specializations.name: Go-to-market / new market launch
specializations.why: Companies expanding into a new region or segment need AEs who can build a pipeline from nothing rather than inherit one, and this experience is a distinct line item on a resume that gets noticed.

specializations.name: Channel and partner sales
specializations.why: Selling through resellers or partners instead of direct to buyers is a different skill set (negotiation with a party who isn't the end user) and is consistently under-supplied relative to demand.

pros: The job has a clean scoreboard: you know by Friday whether the week worked, which is more clarity than most jobs offer.
Closing a deal that's been stuck for weeks is an immediate, specific kind of satisfaction that doesn't wear off with repetition.
Commission and equity are common enough in postings that strong performance shows up in your paycheck the same quarter, not years later.
The skills transfer almost everywhere: sales, negotiation, and forecasting are wanted across industries, so a good AE is rarely stuck at one company or sector.
cons: The number resets to zero every quarter or year, so a great close last month buys you nothing this month.
A lot of the week is spent on people who will never buy, and knowing that in advance doesn't make the calls faster.
CRM upkeep is unglamorous and constant, and skipping it catches up with you at forecast time.
Quarter-end and year-end weeks can run long and unpredictable, which is hard to plan personal life around a few times a year.

faq.q: how long does it take to become an account executive
faq.a: Most people spend 1 to 2 years as an SDR or junior sales rep first, then another 1 to 2 years closing full-cycle deals before landing a proper AE title, putting the realistic timeline around 3 to 5 years. The median AE already has 5 years of experience, so this is not treated as an entry-level title even where the degree requirement is soft.

faq.q: can you become an account executive without a degree
faq.a: Yes, in practice: while 82% of postings list a degree requirement, 26% waive it, and what gets you hired is a documented track record of quota attainment. A strong run as an SDR or sales rep with real numbers to show tends to outweigh the absence of a diploma.

faq.q: account executive vs account manager, what's the difference
faq.a: An account executive is paid to open new revenue and close deals; an account manager is paid to retain and grow an existing account after the sale. The two roles sit on opposite ends of the same customer relationship, and companies usually hire and comp them separately.

faq.q: is account executive a good career right now
faq.a: The pay range runs wide (the middle of the market sits around $152k, with the top quarter well above that), and the skills carry across industries and company sizes. The tradeoff is a quota that resets constantly, so it suits people who like being measured more than it suits people who want quiet, steady weeks.

faq.q: can an account executive job be done remotely
faq.a: Often, yes: 42% of postings are remote, since the core work (calls, CRM, proposals) doesn't require a physical office. Enterprise and strategic roles are more likely to require some travel for in-person pitches or renewals, even when the base role is listed as remote.
